title: Ethiopian Fresh Cheese
community: All of Ethiopia — the fresh cheese of the celebration table
author: Mama Tigist
desc: Ethiopian Ayib — fresh milk heated with lemon juice or vinegar until curdled, then drained through cloth into a soft, mild fresh cheese. The essential companion to kitfo, gomen, and the celebration platter — its cool mildness tempers the heat of berbere and mitmita.
longDesc: Ayib is the cool counterbalance on the Ethiopian table — the mild, fresh cheese that tempers the intense heat of berbere and mitmita. Served alongside kitfo, it is eaten together in every bite, the lactic freshness cutting through the mitmita's fierce heat. Made in 2 hours from milk and a souring agent.
ingredients: 4 tbsp lemon juice or white wine vinegar
steps: Heat milk over medium heat to 85°C — steaming but not boiling.
Add lemon juice or vinegar. Stir once.
Remove from heat. Rest 10 minutes — the curds will separate from the whey.
Line a sieve with muslin cloth.
Pour curdled milk into the cloth.
chefTips: The milk should be at 85°C — too cool and curds won't form; too hot and they become rubbery.
Do not stir after adding the souring agent — disturbing the curds produces a smaller yield.
Drain for 1 hour for soft ayib; 2 hours for firmer.
cookingScience: Ayib is an acid-precipitated cheese — the lemon juice's citric acid drops the milk's pH below 4.6 (the isoelectric point of casein protein). At this pH, the casein micelles destabilise and aggregate into curds. Unlike rennet-set cheese, acid-set cheese coagulation is rapid and temperature-dependent — above 70°C, the acid coagulation is most complete.
sustainabilityTips: The whey drained from ayib can be used in porridge or bread — zero waste.
servedWith: On the celebration platter alongside all wats
As a cooling accompaniment to hot dishes
healthBenefits: Probiotic potential from natural acid bacteria.
The cool dairy tempers the inflammation from capsaicin.
culturalNote: Ayib is the peacemaker on the Ethiopian table — between the fierce heat of mitmita on kitfo and the tongue, it stands as the cool, mild intermediary. No Ethiopian celebration platter is complete without it, and no piece of kitfo is eaten without a bite of ayib alongside.
